l1_text:
## tsa11-p01
So far, what was taught comes about for one person directly for the attainment of liberation, in the stated compendium manner; for another, through coming into use in the initiation to be taught. Hence initiation and the rest must be taught. (11.1) Therein — "who is the entitled one?" — for that determination, the descent of power is examined. (11.2)
l2_text:
## tsa11-p01 — why initiation comes next
Everything taught so far reaches some people directly — they hear the compendium and are free.
Others can only use it once initiation is on the table. So initiation, and what follows from it,
must now be taught. And the first question is eligibility: who is even entitled to receive it?
That question forces the topic of this chapter — the descent of power.
*Fidelity: preserved (frame + entitlement question + topic-setting). Added: nothing (no SUPPLIED).*

CITATION_GROUNDING: 'puruṣa' used in candidate but not in source

c1.body:
This passage frames the whole chapter. Everything taught so far serves some people directly for liberation — they hear the compendium and are free. Others can only use it once initiation is on the table. So initiation, and what follows from it, must now be taught. And the first question is eligibility: who is entitled to receive it? That question is not procedural (who may be initiated) but causal (what makes one capable of receiving it) — and it forces the topic of this ahnika: the descent of power. Nothing is yet asserted about grace; the question is opened, not answered, and the pūrvapakṣa follows.

The passage has two sentences and one question. First, the frame: what was taught so far reaches some directly for liberation in the stated compendium manner; for others, it reaches only through coming into use in the initiation to be taught. Hence initiation and the rest must be taught. The "and the rest" (dīkṣādikam) signals that initiation is the door to a whole sequence (snāna, yāga, putraka, sadyaḥ, parokṣa, liṅgoddhāra, abhiṣeka, antyeṣṭi, conduct) that follows in A12–A20. Second, the question: "who is the entitled one?" (kaḥ adhikārī) — and for that determination (nirūpaṇārtham), the descent of power is examined (śaktipāto vicāryate). The shift from "who may be initiated" to "what makes one capable" is the ahnika's pivot: eligibility is not a permission but a causal capacity, and the cause of that capacity is śaktipāta. Nothing is yet asserted about grace; the question is opened and the pūrvapakṣa (three theories) follows in P2.
c1.terms: adhikārin (entitled recipient), apavarga (liberation), saṃgraha-nīti (compendium manner), vaktavyam (must be taught), vicāryate (is examined).
c1.see_also: A10 (kalādhvā), A12 (snāna, bath before initiation), spans TS11.1–11.2.
c1.function: Frame-setting and topic-introduction. Establishes why śaktipāta, not initiation itself, is the ahnika's subject, and why eligibility is a causal question.
c1.local_context: Opening of the ahnika; follows A10's kalādhvā (digit-course) and precedes the pūrvapakṣa in P2.
c1.boundary: No doctrine stated; the pūrvapakṣa theories follow in P2. No unresolved items beyond the frame.

l1_text:
## tsa11-p02
Therein, some say: "Since, from absence of knowledge, saṃsāra is ignorance-rooted, on its removal there is the descent of power through the rise of knowledge." For them, it must be stated that the very rise of right knowledge is defective. If [descent were] produced by karma, then, like a fruit of karma, there would be contingency of being enjoyed; and if, for the enjoyer, a descent of power is admitted, there is over-extension. But if the rise of knowledge is caused by the Lord's will, there is mutual dependence, and futility, and contingency of passion and the rest in the Lord. (11.3a) "If it is said: from mutual obstruction of two equal opposed karmas there is equilibrium of karma, thence the descent of power" — no: where there is succession, opposition is impossible; and even where there is opposition, there is contingency that another unopposed karma gives enjoyment; and if unopposed karma does not proceed, then and there is contingency of the body's fall. If it is said that birth-and-life-span-giving karma is not obstructed but only enjoyment-giving karma is obstructed — whence is that? If that karma exists, and power were to descend, what would it fear from the enjoyment-giver? (11.3b)
l2_text:
## tsa11-p02 — the failed explanations
Three theories are on offer, and Abhinava demolishes each in turn. Some say liberation is a matter
of knowledge: we suffer from not-knowing, so when knowledge dawns, power descends. But the "dawn
of right knowledge" is itself the thing that needs explaining — the account is circular on arrival.
Say instead that grace is produced by ritual action, and it inherits action's limits: like any reward,
it would be something merely enjoyed, and anyone enjoying anything would count as graced — the
concept explodes. Say it comes from the Lord's sheer will, and knowledge's dawn either grounds the
will (circular again) or floats free of it (pointless) — while saddling the Lord himself with
motive and partiality. A subtler version: when two equal and opposite deeds deadlock, their
equilibrium lets grace through. But deadlock needs simultaneity; deeds ripen in sequence, where
"opposition" has no grip. And even granted the deadlock, some third, unopposed deed would still be
delivering its pleasures — or, if no deed is operating at all, the body should drop on the spot.
Plead that birth-and-lifespan deeds run on while only pleasure-deeds jam: on what ground? If the
deed-structure is intact, what exactly would descending power be afraid of in the pleasure-giver?
*Fidelity: preserved (three theories + replies in order). Added: "circular on arrival" unpacks
anyonyāśraya [SUPPLIED-structural]. Not-resolved: the "defective" charge against right knowledge
is promissory here (iti vācyam).*

CITATION_GROUNDING: all technical terms grounded in source

c1.body:
Three theories of descent are proposed and each demolished. First, the knowledge-theory: saṃsāra is ignorance-rooted, so when knowledge dawns, power descends. But "the dawn of right knowledge" is itself the unexplained term (the charge is promissory here — iti vācyam); and if karma-produced, enjoyment-contingency (bhogatva-prasaṅga) and over-extension (atiprasaṅga) follow; if Lord's-will-caused, mutual dependence (anyonyāśrayatā), futility (vaiyarthya), and passion in the Lord (rāgādi-prasaṅga). Second, the karma-equilibrium theory: equal opposed karmas deadlock, grace slips through. But succession excludes opposition; a third unopposed karma would still deliver pleasure; or the body should fall on the spot. The "whence?" (kutaḥ?) marks the point: no theory can state its own ground. Third, stain-maturation (P3). Each proposal collapses under its own consequences.

Abhinava does not argue against grace but against every proposed mechanism of grace. The knowledge-theory is circular: samyak-jñānodaya is itself "defective" (vikṛta) — the charge is promissory here (iti vācyam), answered later. If grace is karma-produced, it inherits action's limits: like any reward, it would be merely enjoyed, and anyone enjoying anything would count as graced — the concept explodes (atiprasaṅga). If grace comes from the Lord's will, knowledge's dawn either grounds the will (circular again) or floats free of it (pointless) — while saddling the Lord with motive and partiality (rāgādi-prasaṅga). The karma-equilibrium theory: when two equal and opposed deeds deadlock, their equilibrium lets grace through. But deadlock needs simultaneity; deeds ripen in sequence, where "opposition" has no grip (kramikatve virodhāyogāt). And even granted the deadlock, some third, unopposed deed would still be delivering its pleasures (bhogadāna-prasaṅga) — or, if no deed is operating at all, the body should drop on the spot (dehapāta-prasaṅga). Plead that birth-and-lifespan deeds run on while only pleasure-deeds jam: on what ground? (kutaḥ?) If the deed-structure is intact, what exactly would descending power be afraid of in the pleasure-giver? The repeated "whence?" marks the point: no theory can state its own ground.
c1.terms: karmasāmya (equilibrium of karma), atiprasaṅga (over-extension), anyonyāśraya (mutual dependence), vaiyarthya (futility), kramikatva (succession), jātyāyuṣprada (birth-and-lifespan-giving).
c1.function: Pūrvapakṣa demolition. Clears the ground for the siddhānta in P4 by showing that no proposed mechanism (knowledge, karma, equilibrium) can account for grace.
c1.local_context: Immediately after the framing (P1); the siddhānta begins at P4.
c1.boundary: The "defective" charge against right knowledge is promissory (iti vācyam); answered in later ahnikas. kiṃsvarūpa/kiṃnimitta hang until P3/P4.

l1_text:
## tsa11-p03
"Then, at the maturation of stain there is the descent of power." But that too — of what nature is it, and what is its cause? By this [refutation]: dispassion, special dharma, discrimination, service of the good, attainment of the good, worship of gods and the rest as cause — is refuted. Thus, for dualists, everything is incoherent. (11.4)
l2_text:
## tsa11-p03 — maturation, and the collapse of dualism
"Grace comes when the stain ripens." Very well: what is this ripening — what is it, and what causes
it? No answer comes. And with it fall the whole catalogue of supposed causes — dispassion, merit,
discernment, good company, attainment, worship. For the dualist schools, every option on the table
is now incoherent.
*Fidelity: preserved (maturation challenge + hetu-list + verdict). Added: nothing.*

CITATION_GROUNDING: all technical terms grounded in source

c1.body:
"Grace comes when the stain ripens." The challenge stands: what is this ripening — what is it, and what causes it? The whole catalogue of proposed causes (dispassion, merit, discernment, good company, attainment, worship) is refuted. For dualist schools, every option on the table is incoherent. The theory cannot state its own nature, cause, or means — the same move as P2 but aimed at a single theory. The hetu-list refutation shows that no moral or ritual achievement causes grace; hence grace is not merit-earned.

"At-the-maturation-of-stain, the descent" — but that too: of what nature is it, and what is its cause? (kiṃsvarūpaḥ? kiṃ ca tasya nimittam?) No answer comes. And with it fall the whole catalogue of supposed causes — dispassion (vairāgya), special dharma (dharmaviśeṣa), discrimination (viveka), service of the good (satsevā), attainment of the good (satprāpti), worship of gods (devapūjā) and the rest — refuted (pratyukta). Thus, for dualists (bhedavādin), everything is incoherent (sarvam asamañjasam). The theory cannot state its own nature, cause, or means — the same move as P2 but aimed at a single theory. The hetu-list refutation shows that no moral or ritual achievement causes grace; hence grace is not merit-earned. This is the pūrvapakṣa's last stand; the siddhānta opens at P4 with autonomy.
c1.terms: malaparipāka (stain-maturation), kiṃsvarūpa (of what nature), kiṃnimitta (what cause), hetu (cause), bhedavāda (dualism), asamañjasa (incoherent).
c1.function: Closes the pūrvapakṣa. The siddhānta begins at P4.
c1.local_context: P2–P3 are the refutation half; P4 opens the siddhānta.
c1.boundary: Nature and cause questions left hanging — answered only by the coming siddhānta (P4). The "defective" charge (P2) also remains promissory.

l1_text:
## tsa11-p04
But in the nondual autonomous-supreme-Lord doctrine, this holds. As the Lord, by the play of self-concealment, has become bound soul, person, atom — and there is no contradiction from difference of place, time, or nature — so, by the removal of the concealment of own nature, resorting to the attainment of own nature suddenly or gradually, the atom is called the recipient of the descent of power. And he, the supreme Śiva whose essence is sheer autonomy, is the descender of power. Hence the descent of power is unconditioned indeed — that whose fruit is the manifestation of own nature. But that [descent] for one eager for enjoyment is karma-conditioned. For one eager for transcendent enjoyment, that same descent — through Rudra, Viṣṇu, Brahmā and the rest, the lords over those within Māyā's womb impelled by the Lord's will — taking the form of mantra and the rest, granting discrimination of Māyā and person, of person and śakti, of person and prakṛti, of person and intellect, and other fruit, obstructs the enjoyment of the lower principles. For one eager for both enjoyment and liberation, in enjoyment it is karma-conditioned, in liberation unconditioned. Thus it is both conditioned and unconditioned. (11.5) Nor may it be asked, "Why does the descent of power occur in just this person?" — that same Lord shines thus. When being is thus, what is this "person" for whose sake this object-directed question is raised? (11.6) And this descent of power is ninefold: of the intense, moderate, and mild, through the threefoldness of excess, middleness, and deficiency. Therein, from the utmost intense, then and there at the fall of the body there is identity with the Lord. From the middle intense there is the rise of intuitive knowledge, independent of scripture and teacher, self-verified; on its rise, without outer sacrament, the giver of enjoyment and liberation is called the intuitive teacher. For him there is no conventional observance at all. Yet herein too gradation exists, through diversity of will. Thus, even with intuitiveness, regard for scripture and the rest may occur, for the sake of concord. Hence the with-and-without-ground and many-formed-ness of the intuitive teacher is taught in the scriptures. In every case the intuitive portion is stronger; in its presence, for others there is non-entitlement. (11.7)
l2_text:
## tsa11-p04 — autonomy: the doctrine
Here is Abhinava's own position, and it needs no patch from the wreckage above. The Lord, playing
at hiding himself, has become the bound soul, the person, the atom — and place, time, and
particular nature don't contradict this, since they are his own display. In exactly the same way,
when the hiding lifts and one's own nature is recovered — in a flash or by degrees — the atom is
what we call "a recipient of the descent." And the one from whom it descends is supreme Śiva,
whose whole essence is autonomy. So the descent, whose fruit is simply nature showing itself, is
unconditioned. [SUPPLIED: "simply" — the Sanskrit has svarūpaprathāphala, manifestation-of-own-
nature-as-fruit; "simply" marks that nothing is added.]
Qualifications follow the fruit, not the mechanism. Wanting pleasure? Then karma conditions apply.
Wanting a higher pleasure? Then the very same descent comes down through Rudra, Viṣṇu, Brahmā —
the lords posted inside Māyā's womb at the Lord's will — wearing the shape of mantra and the rest,
teaching apart Māyā from person, person from power, from nature, from intellect, and barring the
way down to a lower enjoyment. Wanting both pleasure and freedom? Then conditioned in the pleasure,
unconditioned in the freedom — both at once.
"But why this person and not that?" The question assumes a "person" standing outside being, waiting
to be picked. There is none: the Lord shines this way, and that shining is all there is.
The descent is ninefold — intense, moderate, mild, each in excess, middle, and deficient measure.
At the peak of intensity, the body drops and there is identity with the Lord then and there. At
middle intensity, intuitive knowledge dawns needing no book and no teacher, self-certifying — and
with it the intuitive teacher, who gives pleasure and freedom with no outer rite at all. Such a
one is bound by no observance. Yet ranks remain, because will differs: even the intuitive may honor
scripture, for agreement's sake — which is why the books describe the intuitive teacher in many
forms, grounded and groundless. In every case the intuitive share outweighs; where it is present,
nothing else confers standing.
*Fidelity: preserved (play-analogy, conditioning rule, why-this-person dissolution, ninefold table).
Added: bracketed SUPPLIED above; "books" for āgameṣu. Not-resolved: nirbhitti/sabhitti forms per
scriptures (external).*

The descent is ninefold — intense, moderate, mild, each in excess, middle, and deficient measure. At the peak of intensity, the body drops and there is identity with the Lord then and there. The passage moves in six steps. (1) The play-analogy: the Lord, playing at hiding himself, has become the bound soul, the person, the atom — and place, time, and particular nature don't contradict this, since they are his own display. (2) In exactly the same way, when the hiding lifts and one's own nature is recovered — in a flash or by degrees — the atom becomes what we call "a recipient of the descent." (3) The one from whom it descends is supreme Śiva, whose whole essence is autonomy; so the descent, whose fruit is simply nature showing itself, is unconditioned. (4) Qualifications follow the fruit, not the mechanism: pleasure → karma-conditioned; higher pleasure → conditioned through Rudra/Viṣṇu/Brahmā (Māyā-womb lords, Lord's-will-impelled, teaching apart Māyā/person/power/nature/intellect, barring lower enjoyment); both → conditioned in pleasure, unconditioned in freedom. (5) "But why this person and not that?" — the question assumes a "person" standing outside being, waiting to be picked; there is none: the Lord shines this way, and that shining is all there is. (6) The ninefold typology (11.7): intense/moderate/mild × excess/middle/deficiency — with distinct fates (utmost-intense → dehapāta = parameśatā; middle-intense → prātibhajñāna, sacrament-free prātibha-guru; gradation persists via icchāvaicitrya; pratibhāṃśa decisive over others).

l1_text:
## tsa11-p05
As in the difference-view, in the presence of beginningless Śiva: for the liberated Śivas, in the functions of creation, dissolution, and the rest, from a mild-intense descent of power there comes the will to go toward a true teacher; toward a false teacher there is only concealment. And going from a false teacher to a true teacher is itself from the descent of power. (11.8) The true teacher is full of the knowledge of the principles of all this scripture — Lord Bhairava the Blessed himself. Even a yogin, by well-practised knowledge alone, has liberating power; therein, fitness is useless, like possession of good fortune, charm, and the rest. (11.9) The false teacher is simply everyone else. (11.10)
l2_text:
## tsa11-p05 — the true teacher
The same pattern holds among the liberated ones: where Śiva's presence is beginningless, a
mild-intense descent moves them to create and dissolve — and to want a true teacher. Toward a
false teacher there is only further hiding; and even the move from a false teacher to a true one
is itself the descent at work. The true teacher knows this scripture's principles whole — he is
Lord Bhairava in person. A yogin too, by knowledge well practised, can set others free; being
"qualified" in the worldly sense — luck, charm, credentials — is as irrelevant as good looks are
to arithmetic. A false teacher is anyone else.
*Fidelity: preserved. Added: the arithmetic simile unpacks saubhāgya-illustration [SUPPLIED-structural].*

c1.body:
The same pattern holds among the liberated ones: a mild-intense descent moves them to want a true teacher; toward a false teacher there is only further concealment; and the move from false to true is itself descent's effect. The true teacher knows this scripture's principles whole — he is Lord Bhairava in person. A yogin too can liberate by well-practised knowledge; worldly fitness (luck, charm, credentials) is as irrelevant as good looks are to arithmetic. A false teacher is anyone else.

The passage moves in three steps. (1) The same pattern among liberated ones: where Śiva's presence is beginningless, a mild-intense descent moves them to create and dissolve — and to want a true teacher. Toward a false teacher there is only further hiding (tirobhāva eva); and even the move from a false teacher to a true one is itself from the descent (śaktipātād eva). (2) The true teacher: full of the knowledge of the principles of all this scripture (samastaitacchāstratattvajñānapūrṇaḥ) — Lord Bhairava the Blessed himself (sākṣāt bhagavadbhairavabhaṭṭārakaḥ eva). Even a yogin, by well-practised knowledge alone (svabhyastajñānatayaiva), has liberating power (mocakatve); therein, fitness (yogyatva) is useless, like possession of good fortune, charm, and the rest (saubhāgyalāvaṇyādimattvasya iva) — the arithmetic analogy unpacked in L2. (3) The false teacher is simply everyone else (anyaḥ sarvaḥ eva).

c1.function: Teacher-criterion. Separates authority (fullness of knowledge) from office or worldly qualification.
c1.local_context: Follows P4's ninefold typology; P6 takes up initiation.
c1.boundary: None major. The saubhāgya-irrelevance is stated by analogy; its force is rhetorical, not argued.

l1_text:
## tsa11-p06
Thus the wisher obtains from the teacher the knowledge-characterized initiation, by which he is liberated instantly, even while alive. Here there are varieties: by glance, by speech, by scriptural instruction, by showing of conduct, by giving of food, and so on. (11.11) Or the practitioner then instantly obtains the life-severing initiation — but that is to be performed only at the moment of death, as will be taught. (11.12) From the utmost three intense [descents] of the intense descent of power, even one who is initiated has no firm conviction of the Śiva-nature of his own self; but by the maturation of conviction, at the end of the body he is Śiva indeed. From the middle moderate, though desiring Śiva-hood he desires enjoyment — he is a fit vessel of knowledge in that same initiation; and he, by the practice of yoga, having enjoyed enjoyment with this very body, at the end of the body is Śiva indeed. (11.13)
l2_text:
## tsa11-p06 — how initiation works, and what follows by rank
So the seeker receives from the teacher the initiation whose mark is knowledge — and is free at
once, while still alive. It comes by a glance, a word, a text taught, a conduct shown, food
shared, and more. There is also the initiation that severs the life-breath — but that one is for
the hour of death, as will be taught. From the highest three intensities of the intense, even the
initiated has no steady footing in his own Śiva-nature — but as conviction ripens, at the body's
end he is Śiva, no qualification. From the middle of the moderate: still hungry for pleasure, yet
a fit vessel for knowledge in that very initiation — he enjoys, with this same body, through yoga
practice, and at the body's end he is Śiva.

c1.body:
So the seeker receives from the teacher the initiation whose mark is knowledge — and is free at once, while still alive. It comes by a glance, a word, a text taught, a conduct shown, food shared, and more. There is also the initiation that severs the life-breath — but that one is for the hour of death, as will be taught. From the highest three intensities of the intense, even the initiated has no steady footing in his own Śiva-nature — but as conviction ripens, at the body's end he is Śiva, no qualification. From the middle of the moderate: still hungry for pleasure, yet a fit vessel for knowledge in that very initiation — he enjoys, with this same body, through yoga practice, and at the body's end he is Śiva.

The passage moves in four steps. (1) The wisher obtains from the teacher the knowledge-characterized initiation (jñānalakṣaṇāṃ dīkṣām), by which he is liberated instantly (sadyaḥ eva), even while alive (jīvann api). The varieties: by glance (avalokanāt), by speech (kathanāt), by scriptural instruction (śāstrasambodhanāt), by showing of conduct (caryādarśanāt), by giving of food (carudānāt), and more (ityādayo bhedāḥ). (2) Or the practitioner then instantly obtains the life-severing initiation (prāṇaviyojikāṃ dīkṣām) — but that is to be performed only at the moment of death (maraṇakṣaṇa eva kāryā), as will be taught (iti vakṣyāmaḥ) — deferred to A15/A19. (3) From the utmost three intensities of the intense descent of power (tīvrās tridhā utkṛṣṭamadhyāt): even one who is initiated (kṛtadīkṣāko 'pi) has no firm conviction of the Śiva-nature of his own self (svātmanaḥ śivatāyām na tathā dṛḍhapratipattiḥ); but by the maturation of conviction (pratipattiparipākakrameṇa), at the end of the body (dehānte) he is Śiva indeed (śivaḥ eva). (4) From the middle moderate (madhyamadhyāt): though desiring Śiva-hood (śivatotsuko 'pi), he desires enjoyment (bhogaprepsuḥ) — he is a fit vessel of knowledge (jñānabhājanam) in that same initiation (tathaiva dīkṣāyām); and he, by the practice of yoga (yogābhyāsa), having enjoyed enjoyment (bhuktvā bhogam) with this very body (anenaiva dehena), at the body's end (dehānte) is Śiva indeed (śivaḥ eva).
c1.terms: jñānalakṣaṇā dīkṣā (knowledge-characterized initiation), prāṇaviyojikā (life-severing initiation), maraṇakṣaṇa (moment of death), dṛḍhapratipatti (firm conviction), pratipattiparipāka (maturation of conviction), jñānabhājana (fit vessel of knowledge).
c1.see_also: A11 P4, A12 (snāna), A15 (sadyaḥ), spans TS11.11–11.13.
c1.function: Initiation-types and grade→fate mapping. Establishes that grade determines timing and mode, never the outcome for the entitled.
c1.local_context: P4–P5 established descent and teacher; P6 takes up the rite.
c1.boundary: Prāṇaviyojikā rite deferred (iti vakṣyāmaḥ → A15/A19). The "fit vessel" (jñānabhājana) criterion is asserted, not argued.

l1_text:
## tsa11-p07
From the deficient moderate, having enjoyed enjoyment with another body, he attains Śiva-hood. (11.14) The moderate is threefold: when eagerness for enjoyment has become predominant, then there is mildness — since eagerness there is by way of the Lord's mantra and yoga as means, and since from mantra and yoga of the Lord there is ending in liberation, hence there is descent-nature. (11.15) There too, through gradation, there is threefoldness. Thus this is the principal descent of power. (11.16)
l2_text:
## tsa11-p07 — the mildest operative grade
One step down: pleasure enjoyed in another body, then Śiva-hood. The moderate comes in three:
where hunger for pleasure rules, the grade is mild — for that hunger travels by the Lord's mantra
and yoga, and mantra-yoga ends in freedom, so the structure still counts as descent. Three sub-
ranks within, by the same gradation. This — the whole mild-to-intense span terminating in freedom —
is the principal descent.
*Fidelity: preserved. Added: closing gloss unpacks mukhya (principal = the full operative span).*

c1.body:
One step down from the middle moderate: pleasure enjoyed in another body, then Śiva-hood. The moderate is threefold; where hunger for pleasure rules, the grade is mild — for that hunger travels by the Lord's mantra and yoga, which end in freedom, so the structure still counts as descent. Three sub-ranks within, by the same gradation. This whole mild-to-intense span terminating in freedom is the principal descent (mukhya śaktipāta).

The passage moves in three steps. (1) From deficient-moderate (nikṛṣṭamadhyāt): having enjoyed enjoyment (bhuktvā bhogam) with another body (dehāntareṇa), he attains Śiva-hood (śivatvam eti). (2) The moderate is threefold (madhyas tu tridhā): when eagerness for enjoyment is predominant (bhogotsukatā pradhānabhūtā), then there is mildness (mandatvam) — since eagerness there is by way of the Lord's mantra and yoga as means (pārameśvaramantrayogopāyatayā yatas tatra autsukyam), and since from mantra and yoga of the Lord there is ending in liberation (pārameśamantrayogādeś ca yato mokṣaparyantatvam), hence there is descent-nature (ataḥ śaktipātarūpatā). (3) There too, through gradation (tāratamyāt), there is threefoldness (traividhyam). Thus this — the whole mild-to-intense span terminating in freedom — is the principal descent (ity eṣaḥ mukhyaḥ śaktipātaḥ). "Principal" unpacks in L2: the full operative span, not a single grade.
c1.terms: nikṛṣṭamadhya (deficient-moderate), madhyas tridhā (moderate threefold), bhogotsukatā (eagerness for enjoyment), mandatva (mildness), mukhya śaktipāta (principal descent), tāratamya (gradation).
c1.function: Completes the grade table (utmost/middle/deficient × intense/moderate/mild); defines mukhya śaktipāta.
c1.local_context: P6 gave utmost/middle; P7 closes the moderate band and defines "principal."
c1.boundary: None major. The "principal" gloss is a register choice, flagged for review.

l1_text:
## tsa11-p08
For Vaiṣṇavas and the rest, as with royal favor, there is no ending in liberation; hence there is no analysis here. (11.17) But the presence of Lord and Śakti is everywhere — so it has been stated. That is not the eldest, but the fierce or the fiercer. This descent of power, though varied, divides through variety of gradation: some Vaiṣṇava-dweller, by the samayin course, attaining maturation in the five streams, reaches supreme entitlement to the all-transcending sixfold scripture of the Lord; another, by the leap-course, with endless difference; some, without sequence. Hence therefore even teachers of lower-lower doctrines are here non-entitled, even to the mere showing of the maṇḍala; but a teacher of the upper doctrine enlivens even the lower-lower doctrine, through fullness — hence he is all-entitled. (11.18) He is the deśika, the guru, the ācārya, the initiator, the cumbaka. And he, fully knowledgeable indeed, is supreme — for without him there is no success of initiation and the rest. (11.19)
l2_text:
## tsa11-p08 — outsiders and the teacher who contains all ranks
What of the Vaiṣṇavas and the rest? Their grace is like the king's favor — real, but it doesn't
end in freedom. So no analysis here. (That said, Lord-and-Śakti are present everywhere — only not
as "the eldest"; she is Fierce, and Fiercer.) The descent varies, and its varieties sort by rank:
one Vaiṣṇava practitioner, ripened through the samayin course and the five streams, rises to the
highest charge of the Lord's all-surpassing sixfold word; another takes the leap, endlessly
variegated; another, no stages at all. Hence: teachers of the lowest doctrines have no standing
here — not even to display a maṇḍala. But a teacher of the height, by sheer completeness, gives
life even to the lowest doctrine. He is deśika, guru, ācārya, initiator, cumbaka — five names for
one plenitude. And he, knowing fully, outranks all: without him no initiation succeeds.
*Fidelity: preserved. Added: "the king's favor" kept literal (rājānugrahavat). Not-resolved:
srotaḥpañcaka/ṣaḍardha technicals assumed (external).*

c1.body:
What of the Vaiṣṇavas and the rest? Their grace is like the king's favor — real, but no ending in freedom; so no analysis here. Lord-and-Śakti present everywhere, but not as "the eldest" — she is Fierce, and Fiercer. The descent varies: samayin/five-streams Vaiṣṇava → highest charge of the sixfold word; leap-course; no stages. Lower-lower teachers have no standing; an upper teacher, by completeness, enlivens even the lowest. Five teacher-names for one plenitude; without him no initiation succeeds.

The passage moves in four steps. (1) Outsiders: for Vaiṣṇavas and the rest, as with royal favor (rājānugrahavat), there is no ending in liberation (na mokṣāntatā) — hence no analysis here (na iha vivecanam). (2) Lord-and-Śakti presence everywhere (śivaśaktyadhiṣṭhānam sarvatra), as stated; but that is not the eldest (na jyeṣṭhā), rather fierce or fiercer (ghorā ghoratarā vā). (3) The descent varies (vicitro 'pi), divides by variety of gradation (tāratamyavaicitryāt): some Vaiṣṇava-dweller (kaścid vaiṣṇavādisthaḥ), by samayin-course (samayyādikrameṇa), in the five-streams (srotaḥpañcake), attaining maturation (prāptaparipākaḥ), reaches supreme entitlement to the all-transcending sixfold scripture (sarvottīrṇabhagavatṣaḍardhaśāstraparamādhikāritām); another by leap-course (ullaṅghanakrameṇa) with endless difference (anantabhedena); some without sequence (akramam). (4) Hence: teachers of lower-lower doctrines (adharādharaśāsanasthā guravo 'pi) are non-entitled here (anadhikāriṇaḥ iha), even to mere maṇḍala-showing (maṇḍalamātradarśane 'pi); but a teacher of the upper doctrine (ūrdhvaśāsanasthas tu guruḥ), by fullness (pūrṇatvāt), enlivens even the lower-lower doctrine (adharādharaśāsanam prāṇayati) — hence all-entitled (sarvādhikārī). He is deśika, guru, ācārya, dīkṣaka, cumbaka — five names for one plenitude. And he, fully knowledgeable (pūrṇajñānaḥ eva), is supreme (sarvottamaḥ) — for without him (tena vinā) there is no success of initiation and the rest (dīkṣādyasampatteḥ).

l1_text:
## tsa11-p09
The yogin is fit if, for one eager for fruit, he is able to give the fruit without interval through teaching of means; through teaching of means he is fit in knowledge alone, and in liberation too through approaching; and desiring fullness of knowledge, one may take even many teachers. (11.20) According to differences of knowledge, higher and highest, one should conduct oneself among them. But in abandoning a teacher of complete knowledge there is expiation itself. (11.21) "But is one who says nothing, or says the reverse, not to be abandoned?" — "Never," we say. For by his very full knowledge there is absence of passion and the rest. Hence silence and the rest must come from some cause residing in the pupil — such as unfitness or distrust. Hence the pupil must strive in his service, not in his abandonment. (11.22)
l2_text:
## tsa11-p09 — the yogin, many teachers, and the ban on abandonment
A yogin is fit to take on when he can deliver the goods at once, by teaching the means — fit in
bare knowledge by that teaching, and in freedom too, by whoever comes close. Wanting fuller
knowledge, take even many teachers, and move among them by the rank of their knowing. One thing
is forbidden: dropping a teacher who knows completely — that itself needs expiation. "But what of
a teacher who goes silent, or teaches wrong — may he not be dropped?" Never, says Abhinava: one
who knows fully has no lust or hate left to explain the silence. So the silence comes from
something on the pupil's side — unfitness, distrust. Work harder at serving him; do not work at
leaving him.
*Fidelity: preserved (fitness rule, many-teacher rule, nanu + reply). Added: dialogue voicing.*

CITATION_GROUNDING: 'ātman' used in candidate but not in source

c1.body:
A yogin is fit to take on when he can deliver the goods at once, by teaching the means — fit in bare knowledge by that teaching, and in freedom too, by whoever comes close. Wanting fuller knowledge, take even many teachers, and move among them by the rank of their knowing. One thing forbidden: dropping a teacher who knows completely — that itself needs expiation. "But what of a teacher who goes silent, or teaches wrong?" Never: full knowledge means no lust or hate; the silence comes from something on the pupil's side (unfitness, distrust). Work harder at serving him; do not work at leaving him.

The passage moves in three steps. (1) The yogin's fitness: fit to take on (yuktaḥ) if, for one eager for fruit (phalotsukasya), able to give fruit immediately (avyavahitam eva phalaṃ dātum) through teaching of means (upāyopadeśena); through teaching of means, fit in knowledge alone (jñāne eva yuktaḥ), and in liberation too (mokṣe 'pi) through approaching (abhyupāyāt); desiring fullness of knowledge (jñānapūrṇatākāṅkṣī), may take even many teachers (bahūn api gurūn). (2) Conduct among teachers: according to differences of knowledge, higher and highest (uttamottamādijñānabhedāpekṣayā), one should conduct oneself (varteta) among them. But abandoning a teacher of complete knowledge (sampūrṇajñānagurutyāge) brings expiation itself (prāyaścittam eva). (3) The nanu + reply: "But is one who says nothing, or says the reverse, not to be abandoned?" (nanu so 'pi abruvan viparītaṃ vā bruvan kiṃ na tyājyaḥ?) — "Never" (naiva), we say (iti brūmaḥ). For by his very full knowledge (tasya hi pūrṇajñānatvāt eva) there is absence of passion and the rest (rāgādyabhāvaḥ). Hence silence and the rest must come from some cause residing in the pupil (śiṣyagatenaiva kenacit nimittena) — such as unfitness or distrust (ayogyatvānāśvastatvādinā). Hence the pupil must strive in his service (tadupāsane yatanīyam śiṣyeṇa), not in his abandonment (na tattyāge).
c1.terms: phalotsuka (fruit-eager), avyavahita (without interval), upāyopadeśa (teaching of means), sampūrṇajñāna (complete knowledge), prāyaścitta (expiation), ayogyatva (unfitness), anāśvastatva (distrust).
c1.function: Fitness rule, many-teacher rule, no-abandonment ruling (via nanu + reply).
c1.boundary: None major (practical ruling). The reply's force depends on the premise (no rāga in the fully-knowing); if the premise fails, the ruling fails.

## tsa11-p10
Thus the descent of power, the cause of grace, is unconditioned indeed, disregarding karma, destiny, and the rest. (11.23) Concealment: concealment has as its fruit the partaking in dense suffering and delusion conditioned by karma and the rest. As by the autonomy of light the awakened one, though behaving like the deluded, inwardly censures deluded conduct, so the deluded one may perform awakened conduct such as worship of mantra and the rest, and censure it. And as his deluded conduct, though performed, perishes for the awakened one, so his awakened conduct — being censured, of the nature of forbidden conduct, apprehensive through itself — drowns him in the mud of suffering and delusion. l2_text:
## tsa11-p10 — grace unconditioned; hiding; the unbroken self
So: the descent, which is what makes grace happen, is unconditioned — it does not wait on deeds
or destinies. Hiding, by contrast, ripens thick suffering and confusion, all of it deed-
conditioned. Watch the mirror: the awake man playing the fool still inwardly despises folly — and
the fool playing awake, mouthing mantras, still despises the part. The awake man's folly, once
acted, dissolves; but the fool's acted awakeness — performed yet inwardly condemned, forbidden in
form, making him suspect even to himself — sinks him in the mud. For one in whom the descent has
risen, there is no hiding. And here too, stop weighing deeds — as before. Even then, will differs:
one may yet taste suffering with this very body — like those who both serve and revile the
initiation, the conduct, the teacher, the god, the fire, or like old Śaivas who walked away. And

c1.body:
The descent, cause of grace, is unconditioned — it does not wait on deeds or destinies. Concealment, by contrast, ripens thick suffering and confusion, all deed-conditioned. The mirror simile: the awake man playing the fool still inwardly despises folly; the fool playing awake, mouthing mantras, still despises the part — and the fool's acted awakeness, performed yet inwardly condemned, sinks him in the mud. For one in whom descent has risen, no hiding. And here too, stop weighing deeds — as before. Even then, will differs: one may yet taste suffering with this body (double-dealers, apostates). And even then, by that same differing will: the hidden one may join the descent himself — or, dead, through kin or teacher's grace. Holding to "the doings are mine, and I am the Lord" — never see the self as broken.

The passage moves in four steps. (1) Grace unconditioned: the descent (śaktipātaḥ), cause of grace (anugrahanimittam), is unconditioned indeed (nirapekṣaḥ eva) — disregarding karma, destiny, and the rest (karmādiniyatyapekṣaṇāt). (2) Concealment (tirobhāvaḥ): concealment has as its fruit (phalatva) the partaking in dense suffering and delusion (gāḍhaduḥkhamohabhāgitva) conditioned by karma and the rest (karmādyapekṣa). The mirror simile: by light's autonomy (prakāśasvātantryāt) the awakened (prabuddhaḥ) though behaving like the deluded (mūḍhavat ceṣṭate) inwardly censures deluded conduct (hṛdayena nindati mūḍhaceṣṭām); so the deluded (mūḍho 'pi) may perform awakened conduct such as mantra-worship (mantrārādhanādikām) and censure it (nindec ca). And as his deluded conduct, though performed (kriyamāṇāpi), perishes for the awakened (prabuddhasya dhvaṃsam eti) — so his awakened conduct, being censured (nindyamānā), of forbidden-conduct nature (niṣiddhācaraṇarūpatvāt), self-apprehensive through itself (svayaṃ ca tayā eva viśaṅkamānatvāt), drowns him (enam nimajjayati) in suffering-delusion-mud (duḥkhamohapaṅke). (3) But for one in whom descent has arisen (utpannaśaktipātasya tu) there is no concealment (na tirobhāvo 'sti). Here too, regard for karma is to be denied (niṣedhyā), as before (pūrvavat). There too, through will-diversity (icchāvaicitryāt): fruition of suffering with this body only (etaddehamātropabhogyaduḥkhaphalatvam vā) — as for those given to both service and censure toward initiation/conduct/teacher/god/fire (sevānindanobhayaprasaktānām iva) and as for former Śaiva-doctrine-dwellers who abandoned it (prāk śivaśāsanasthānāṃ tattyāginām iva). (4) There too, by will-diversity: though concealed (tirobhūto 'pi), one joins descent (yujyate) oneself (svayaṃ) by descent (śaktipātena), or dead (mṛto vā) through kin/teacher grace (bandhugurvādikṛpāmukhena). Thus (iti evaṃ) reflecting (anusaṃdadhat) act-partaking-in-oneself (kṛtyabhāgitvam svātmani) as the Lord itself (parameśvaraḥ eva), one should not see (na paśyet) the self as broken (khaṇḍitam ātmānam).
